difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the epidemiologist treats a percentage increase as if it were an increase in the absolute number of cases, and buries that move inside an appeal to her own credentials. Students who spot only the ad hominem framing or only the statistical slip miss the interaction.
stimulus: Epidemiologist: As someone who has spent thirty years analyzing outbreak data, I can assure the council that the new pathogen poses a graver threat than the old one. The old pathogen's incidence rose by just 4 percent last year, whereas the new pathogen's incidence rose by 60 percent. Anyone who has not worked in the field, as I have, should hesitate to dispute these numbers.
questionStem: The reasoning in the epidemiologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a comparison of rates of change as if it established a comparison of total case counts, while implying that the speaker's expertise insulates that inference from challenge

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that no other pathogens pose a comparable threat to public health

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between the speaker's expertise and the accuracy of the data cited

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on statistics drawn from a sample that is too small to support a general conclusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that what is true of the new pathogen's incidence must also be true of its mortality rate

explanations.correct: A percentage rise from a small base can still leave the new pathogen's total caseload far below the old one's; the argument slides from rate-of-change to absolute threat, and wards off objections by citing the speaker's experience rather than addressing the inference.
explanations.B: The argument compares only two pathogens; it does not need to rule out others.
explanations.C: The expertise claim is used to deflect disagreement, not to explain why the data are accurate.
explanations.D: Sample size is never characterized; this is a plausible-but-absent flaw.
explanations.E: Mortality is never mentioned; the conclusion is about threat, but the scope-shift at issue is rate-to-absolute, not incidence-to-mortality.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: an appeal to authority (the Nobel laureate) is used to license a scope shift from 'effective in clinical trials' to 'effective in routine practice.' Students who name only the appeal to authority or only the scope shift miss that the authority is doing the work of papering over the shift.
stimulus: Pharmacologist: The new anticoagulant should be prescribed routinely to patients at risk of stroke. Dr. Reyes, a Nobel laureate in medicine, has publicly endorsed the drug, and controlled clinical trials have shown that it reduces clot formation more reliably than the current standard. Her endorsement, together with the trial data, settles the matter.
questionStem: The reasoning in the pharmacologist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that because controlled trial results imply routine effectiveness, a respected endorsement can substitute for evidence of such effectiveness

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that Dr. Reyes's Nobel Prize was awarded in an unrelated field

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a necessary condition for prescribing the drug as a condition sufficient to do so

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from an unrepresentative sample of clinical trial participants

choices.label: E
choices.text: attacks Dr. Reyes's credentials rather than the substance of her endorsement

explanations.correct: Controlled-trial performance and routine-practice performance are different claims; the argument leans on the laureate's endorsement to bridge that gap instead of supplying evidence that trial results carry over. The endorsement and the scope shift work together.
explanations.B: The stimulus never indicates Reyes's field; assuming she is unqualified would be an unsupported gloss on the argument.
explanations.C: No conditional relationship is stated; this is an accurate description of a different, absent flaw.
explanations.E: The argument defers to Reyes; it does not attack her.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the ethicist equivocates on 'natural' (naturally occurring vs. morally natural) and uses that equivocation to collapse a descriptive-to-normative gap. Students who flag only the is/ought move or only the ambiguity miss that each enables the other.
stimulus: Ethicist: Competition among members of a species is found in every biological environment we have studied; it is entirely natural. Whatever is natural in this sense is morally natural as well, since our moral intuitions themselves evolved under selection pressures. It follows that ruthless competition among humans in the marketplace is morally above reproach.
questionStem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: exploits an ambiguity in the term 'natural' in order to move from a claim about what is widespread in nature to a claim about what is morally permissible

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted that what is true of a species as a whole must be true of each of its members

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on evidence drawn exclusively from non-human species

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that moral intuitions cannot be subjected to further critical scrutiny

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a claim about the origins of moral intuitions with a claim about their content

explanations.correct: The first premise uses 'natural' descriptively (occurring in nature); the second premise silently shifts 'natural' into a normative register ('morally natural'); the conclusion then treats the second sense as if it had been established by the first. The equivocation is what makes the is-to-ought leap look licensed.
explanations.B: No part-whole move is in play.
explanations.C: The argument draws on biology generally, including human evolution; the evidentiary scope isn't the issue.
explanations.D: The argument assumes intuitions are trustworthy, but that isn't the structural move at fault.
explanations.E: Tempting — origins-vs-content is nearby — but the argument doesn't isolate 'origins' as its hook; the equivocation on 'natural' is the pivot.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: percentage-vs-absolute confusion hidden inside selection bias. The rise in 'share of claims' could reflect fewer good drivers being insured, not worsening driving. Students who name only the selection bias or only the percentage confusion miss the interaction.
stimulus: Insurance analyst: Drivers under 25 now account for 42 percent of collision claims filed with our company, up from 34 percent five years ago. Over the same period, our company raised premiums for drivers over 50, prompting many of them to switch carriers. It is therefore clear that drivers under 25 have become considerably more dangerous on the road.
questionStem: The reasoning in the insurance analyst's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a change in the behavior of one group from a change in that group's share of a pool whose composition has itself been altered by the speaker's own company

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the claims experience of a single insurance company to that of the industry as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that collision claims are a reliable proxy for collisions

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes without warrant that drivers over 50 are safer than drivers under 25

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a cause of an increase in premiums as if it were an effect of that increase

explanations.correct: When older drivers leave the pool, younger drivers' share of claims can rise even if their absolute claim rate is unchanged. The argument also ignores that its own company caused the compositional shift, so 'more dangerous' isn't warranted.
explanations.B: The scope of the conclusion is plausibly about this company's drivers; even on a broader reading, the central error is the compositional shift.
explanations.C: Plausible-but-absent; no claim-vs-collision distinction is raised.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't rank the groups' safety; it claims under-25s got worse.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: treats evidence about what the framers individually believed as evidence about what the Constitution as a ratified document means — a category error, combined with an appeal to the framers' authority. The trap answer describes ad hominem reversed.
stimulus: Constitutional scholar: Several of the framers wrote privately that they viewed a standing peacetime army as a threat to liberty. Because the framers are the supreme interpretive authorities on the Constitution they drafted, the Constitution, properly read, prohibits the maintenance of such an army. Any judge who rules otherwise is simply ignoring what the document means.
questionStem: The reasoning in the constitutional scholar's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the private views of individual drafters as if they determined the meaning of a ratified legal text, and treats the drafters' authority as settling an interpretive question rather than bearing on it

choices.label: B
choices.text: attacks the character of judges who disagree rather than engaging their legal arguments

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that a document's meaning can change over time without any formal amendment

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a universal conclusion from the views of only a few of the framers

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses what the framers hoped the Constitution would accomplish with what it in fact accomplished

explanations.correct: Private letters are a different object from a ratified text; the scholar collapses that distinction while elevating the framers from relevant authorities to decisive ones. Both moves are needed to reach the conclusion.
explanations.B: Tempting, because the last sentence stings — but the argument targets judges' reasoning, not their character; ad hominem is the wrong label.
explanations.C: The argument implicitly denies meaning can shift; that denial is not the structural flaw.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't quantify how many framers held the view; weakening on 'only a few' would miss the category error.
explanations.E: Hopes-vs-accomplishments isn't the distinction being conflated.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: a necessary/sufficient confusion wrapped in an ad hominem. The columnist discredits opponents to distract from the logical slip between 'without clean water, no civilization' and 'clean water suffices for civilization.'
stimulus: Columnist: Without access to clean water, no ancient civilization ever flourished. Critics who dismiss modern aid programs that focus on water infrastructure are either ignorant of history or indifferent to suffering. The lesson is plain: any region that receives clean water will become a flourishing society.
questionStem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition whose absence precludes an outcome as if its presence were enough to produce the outcome, and deflects objections by impugning the motives of those who raise them

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that ancient civilizations differed in important respects from modern societies

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes, without giving reasons, that clean water programs are the most cost-effective form of aid

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a claim about what has happened with a claim about what ought to happen

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on evidence that is consistent with the denial of the conclusion it is meant to support

explanations.correct: 'Without X, never Y' makes X necessary for Y, not sufficient. The columnist upgrades necessity to sufficiency, and uses a character attack on critics to preempt scrutiny of the upgrade.
explanations.B: Plausible reading, but the flaw isn't ancient-modern disanalogy; even within ancient cases, necessity wouldn't yield sufficiency.
explanations.D: No is/ought confusion; the conclusion is predictive.
explanations.E: Too vague; the conditional slip is the specific error.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the consultant equivocates on 'efficient' (completes tasks quickly vs. delivers business value) and then generalizes from the fastest team to the organization. Students who pick the equivocation miss that generalization isn't at fault; students who pick the generalization miss the term shift.
stimulus: Management consultant: Our internal analytics team is the most efficient group in the company: it closes assigned tickets faster than any other team. Because maximally efficient teams are precisely the ones whose practices generate the greatest business value, the firm should require every department to adopt the analytics team's practices wholesale.
questionStem: The reasoning in the management consultant's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses 'efficient' in one sense to characterize the analytics team and in a different sense to connect efficiency with business value

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a conclusion about every department from evidence about a single department that may not be representative of the others

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that the analytics team's practices cannot be improved upon

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that a correlation between speed and value establishes that speed causes value

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that practices effective within one organization will be effective within another

explanations.correct: The first premise measures efficiency by ticket-closing speed; the bridging premise implicitly treats 'efficient' as meaning 'value-generating.' Without the shift, the conclusion loses its support.
explanations.B: Tempting distractor, but representativeness isn't the issue — the consultant asserts a link between efficiency and value, so the trouble is the word 'efficient,' not sampling.
explanations.D: Causation language doesn't appear; the link is conceptual (via the definition of 'efficient').
explanations.E: The argument is intra-firm, not cross-firm.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: absence-of-evidence inference folded into a scope shift between 'endangered in our surveys' and 'endangered globally.' Students who identify only the absence-of-evidence move miss that the scope shift does most of the damage.
stimulus: Biologist: Our three-year survey of the central rainforest failed to locate a single specimen of the blue-throated tanager. The earlier belief that the species was endangered must therefore be mistaken: had it been endangered, some individuals would surely have appeared in our data. The species is plainly thriving in regions we did not survey.
questionStem: The reasoning in the biologist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers from a failure to detect a species in a limited area that the species must be flourishing in unsurveyed areas

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on survey methods that are not described in sufficient detail to be evaluated

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a three-year period to a conclusion about the species' long-term status

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the belief that the species is endangered as settled rather than as an assumption requiring support

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses being undetected with being extinct

explanations.correct: Not finding a rare species in one area can just mean the species is rare there (consistent with being endangered). The argument treats that absence as evidence of abundance and then leaps to regions it didn't study.
explanations.B: Methodological opacity isn't what the argument turns on.
explanations.C: Time horizon isn't the key move; the spatial leap is.
explanations.D: Reversed — the argument challenges the endangered-status belief, not assumes it.
explanations.E: Opposite of what the argument does: it concludes thriving, not extinction.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: percentage-vs-absolute confusion hidden in statistical language. Declines in 'share of listening time' don't entail declines in hours listened if the overall pie grew; the critic also slips from listening data to 'cultural significance.'
stimulus: Critic: Streaming data show that classical music's share of total listening time fell from 8 percent to 5 percent over the last decade. Since listening is the primary measure of a genre's cultural significance, classical music is undeniably losing cultural significance, and arts foundations should redirect their support accordingly.
questionStem: The reasoning in the critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a decline in a genre's proportion of listening time as establishing a decline in the genre's cultural significance, without ruling out that total listening hours devoted to the genre rose as the overall volume of listening grew

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that streaming data are representative of all forms of music consumption

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that arts foundations have a duty to fund only genres whose listenership is growing

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from a ten-year window to a long-term trend

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the cause of classical music's decline with its effect

explanations.correct: Share can fall while absolute hours rise if the streaming pie grows faster. The critic converts a relative statistic to a claim about absolute cultural significance without addressing that gap.
explanations.B: Plausible-but-absent — representativeness is a different flaw than the stats slip.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't assign foundations a duty; it draws a policy suggestion.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: part-whole (composition) error wrapped in a category confusion. 'Idiomatic' is a property of sentences within a language; the speaker treats it as a property a whole language can have. Students who pick the composition move alone miss the category piece.
stimulus: Linguistics professor: Every competent speaker of English occasionally produces sentences that are idiomatic — expressions whose meanings cannot be predicted from their parts. It follows that English, as a language, is fundamentally idiomatic, and therefore that any formal grammar that assigns meaning compositionally must fail to describe it.
questionStem: The reasoning in the linguistics professor's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a property that can characterize particular sentences within a language as if it were a property that could characterize the language itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that competent speakers are reliable reporters of their own linguistic intuitions

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a feature of English to a feature shared by all natural languages

choices.label: D
choices.text: takes for granted that formal grammars are intended to describe every sentence a speaker might produce

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a sufficient condition for a formal grammar's success with a necessary condition for it

explanations.correct: 'Idiomatic' describes how some sentences behave; calling the language itself idiomatic conflates a sentence-level property with a language-level one — a composition/category slip. The jump to 'compositional grammars must fail' rides on that slip.
explanations.B: Reliability of introspection isn't the structural problem.
explanations.C: The conclusion concerns English only, not all languages.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't hinge on the scope of what grammars aim to cover; it hinges on misapplying 'idiomatic.'
explanations.E: No necessary/sufficient inversion occurs around grammar's success conditions.
